content: In areas with poor sanitation, infections tend to occur later in life. The most common route of transmission is person-to-person contact, although contaminated food and water are also significant sources of infection. There is strong epidemiological evidence supporting waterborne transmission of hepatitis A virus (HAV), more so than for any other virus. Foodborne outbreaks are also relatively common, with sources including infected food handlers, shellfish harvested from contaminated waters, and contaminated produce. Travel from regions with good sanitation to those with poor sanitation poses a high risk of infection. Additionally, infection can be associated with both injecting and non-injecting drug use. Hepatitis A Virus (HAV) and Drinking Water: The transmission of HAV through drinking water supplies is well-documented, and its presence in drinking water represents a significant health risk. The effectiveness of treatment processes for removing HAV must be validated. Drinking water supplies should also be protected from contamination during distribution. Due to the virus's higher resistance to disinfection, Escherichia coli (E. coli) or thermotolerant coliforms are not reliable indicators of HAV presence in drinking water. Hepatitis E Virus (HEV): Hepatitis E virus (HEV) is a single-stranded RNA virus with a non-enveloped icosahedral capsid, measuring 27–34 nm in diameter. HEV shares properties with other viruses, and its classification has evolved over time. It was previously classified under the Caliciviridae family but is now placed in a separate family of hepatitis E-like viruses. HEV exhibits antigenic variation and possibly different serotypes, unlike HAV, which has only one defined serotype. HEV cannot be easily detected or cultivated in conventional cell culture systems, and its identification in environmental samples relies on PCR techniques. HEV causes hepatitis similar to HAV but with a longer incubation period (average 40 days) and a higher mortality rate of up to 25% in pregnant women. In endemic regions, initial infections are more common in young adults than in children. Despite antigenic variation, a single infection appears to provide lifelong immunity. HEV is endemic in certain developing regions, such as India, Nepal, Central Asia, Mexico, and parts of Africa, where it is a leading cause of viral hepatitis. In contrast, clinical cases and outbreaks are rare in regions like Japan, South Africa, the UK, the Americas, Australasia, and Central Europe, despite evidence of the virus's presence. HEV is excreted in the feces of infected individuals and has been detected in raw and treated sewage. Contaminated water has been linked to large outbreaks, including one in Delhi, India, in 1954 (40,000 cases), another in Xinjiang, China, from 1986–1988 (over 100,000 cases), and one in Kanpur, India, in 1991 (79,000 cases). HEV is unique among enteric viruses due to its animal reservoirs, including domestic animals like pigs, cattle, goats, and rodents. Secondary transmission from cases to contacts, including healthcare workers, has been reported but is less common than with HAV. Waterborne outbreaks involving thousands of cases have been documented, emphasizing the role of fecally polluted water in HEV transmission. HEV and Drinking Water: Contaminated water is a confirmed source of HEV, and its presence in drinking water poses a major health risk. While laboratory data on HEV's resistance to disinfection are lacking, evidence from waterborne outbreaks suggests it may be as resistant as other enteric viruses. The effectiveness of treatment processes for removing HEV must be validated. Drinking water supplies should also be protected from contamination during distribution. Due to the virus's likely higher resistance to disinfection, E. coli or thermotolerant coliforms are not reliable indicators of HEV presence in drinking water. Rotaviruses and Orthoreoviruses: Rotaviruses are segmented double-stranded RNA viruses with a non-enveloped icosahedral capsid, measuring 50–65 nm in diameter. The capsid is surrounded by a double-layered shell, giving the virus a wheel-like appearance, hence the name rotavirus. Rotavirus and Orthoreovirus are the two genera of the Reoviridae family associated with human infections. Rotavirus is divided into seven serological groups (A–G), with groups A–C found in humans and group A being the most significant human pathogen. Wild-type group A rotaviruses are not easily grown in cell culture, but PCR-based detection methods are available for environmental testing. Human rotaviruses are the leading cause of infant mortality worldwide, responsible for 50–60% of acute gastroenteritis cases in hospitalized children globally. The virus infects cells in the small intestine, disrupting sodium and glucose transport. Acute infection presents with sudden onset of severe watery diarrhea, fever, abdominal pain, and vomiting, which can lead to dehydration, metabolic acidosis, and potentially fatal outcomes if untreated. The disease burden of rotavirus infections is extremely high. Orthoreoviruses, while infecting many humans, are typically orphan viruses and not associated with significant disease. Rotaviruses and Drinking Water: Rotaviruses are excreted in large quantities (up to 10¹¹ per gram of feces) for about eight days, contaminating domestic sewage and other environments. They have been detected in sewage, rivers, lakes, and treated drinking water. Transmission occurs primarily via the fecal-oral route, with person-to-person spread and inhalation of airborne rotaviruses playing a more significant role than ingestion of contaminated food or water. Although waterborne outbreaks are rare, they have been documented, such as two large outbreaks in China in 1982–1983 linked to contaminated water supplies. Rotaviruses are more resistant to disinfection than other enteric viruses, and the effectiveness of treatment processes must be validated. Protozoan Pathogens: Protozoa and helminths are among the most common causes of infection and disease in humans and animals, with significant public health and socioeconomic impacts. Water plays a critical role in transmitting some of these pathogens. Controlling waterborne transmission is challenging due to the production of resistant cysts, oocysts, or eggs by these organisms, which are difficult to remove through conventional disinfection and filtration processes. Emerging diseases caused by protozoan pathogens, such as cryptosporidiosis, microsporidia, and Cyclospora, have been reported in recent decades. The role of water in transmitting these pathogens may increase as human and animal populations grow and demand for potable water escalates. Acanthamoeba: Acanthamoeba species are free-living amoebae commonly found in aquatic environments and soil. Pathogenic species include A. castellanii, A. polyphaga, and A. culbertsoni. These amoebae can form dormant cysts under unfavorable conditions, which are highly resistant to extreme temperatures, disinfection, and desiccation. A. culbertsoni causes granulomatous amoebic encephalitis, a rare but fatal disease seen in immunocompromised individuals. A. castellanii and A. polyphaga are associated with acanthamoebic keratitis, a painful corneal infection often linked to contact lens use. Acanthamoeba cysts are relatively large and can be removed by filtration, but they are highly resistant to disinfection. Balantidium coli: Balantidium coli is the largest human intestinal protozoan parasite, with trophozoites measuring up to 200 µm. Infections are rare and often asymptomatic, but clinical symptoms can include dysentery, colitis, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. Transmission occurs via the fecal-oral route, often through contact with infected swine or consumption of contaminated water or food. One waterborne outbreak was reported in 1971 due to stormwater runoff containing swine feces. Blastocystis: Blastocystis hominis is a common intestinal parasite with uncertain pathogenicity. It is detected in human fecal samples worldwide, with prevalence rates ranging from 2% to 50%, particularly in developing countries. Transmission is believed to occur via the fecal-oral route, and waterborne transmission has been suggested but not confirmed.
